rv.q: But the two-part, five-hour behemoth that became a blockbuster in London in 2016 and won nine Olivier Awards in 2017 is working its incandescent magic on American audiences.
We emerge having experienced something that Muggles encounter all too rarely: truly transporting theatrical magic.
The staging and special effects are top notch and really well done but the plot is dreadful fanfic that feels like something a 13 year old would write on fanfiction.net in 2007.
The ecstatic hype that accompanies the smash London import to Broadway is amply justified, and then some.
It leaves its audience awestruck, spellbound and deeply satisfied.

It is, at once, a feast of epic theatricality in celebration of the imagination; an immersive coda to the most powerful literary brand of a generation; and a must-see, totally enveloping, thoroughly thrilling chance to experience the global power of shared storytelling at its most robust.
There’s magic in the air throughout this extraordinary production.

Cursed Child is a marvel, a shape-shifting play that effortlessly incorporates music and choreographed movement, classic storytelling and fresh perspectives, a look that incorporates World War II-era Britain and Victorian spiritualism with Hollywood’s latest flash.
At this show’s heart is its humanity, and how it poignantly addresses themes of parental legacy, loss and regret.
That's only the first scene, and already this show feels wondrous.
“Harry Potter and the Cursed Child” remains a theatrical accomplishment of a very rare order.
The Cursed Child is a remarkable and fitting addition to the Potter canon.
If you’re after escape, laughter and a good cry, “Cursed Child” delivers.

The new version, which opened on Tuesday, does feel smaller — its themes starker, its concession to fandom more blatant. But as directed by Tiffany and choreographed by Steven Hoggett, with an essential score from Imogen Heap, it remains diamond-sharp in its staging and dazzling in its visual imagination, as magical as any spell or potion.

As you might imagine, the volume of detail about a fantasy world disgorged over two shows containing some redundant tricks could be particularly wearying to anyone not previously acquainted with Cedric Diggory, or Hagrid the half-giant, or the Ministry of Magic.
To those who have never read a Potter novel or seen a Potter film, “The Cursed Child” will make no sense at all.
Even if you haven’t read the novels, the play is highly enjoyable.
It's more than the best new play of the season.
"Harry Potter and the Cursed Child" on Broadway is a wonder and tickets are going to be tough to come by.

With Harry Potter and the Cursed Child you will not only relish the unsurpassed production values, you will also take away from this truly superlative work a valuable moralizing lesson that is not just limited to the illustrious students of Hogwarts.

"One perfect Broadway play...One of the most extraordinary stage presentations I've ever seen...Ultimately beyond the gorgeous stagecraft, the intriguing plot twists and the beautiful storytelling, this is a tale about fathers and sons...about coming to understand who you are and what you really want to be...
The show gleams like a bolt of lightning — not one that leaves marks on your forehead, just vivid memories in your mind.
This kind of magic, after all, can’t be missed.

The staging is true magic. The creators are up against incredible challenges to recreate the effects of spells and potions, of Floo Powder and Time-Turners and Invisibility Cloaks, with no Hollywood CGI to help them out. And they succeed wildly.
It is still the most magical show on Broadway.
The result is thrilling, thanks in part to enchanting stagecraft — including flying wizards, glowing wands and fantastic spell-casting duels.

We’re better off to live and luxuriate in this electric moment for Broadway, where there is real magic to do, real rarified air to breathe in the majestic Lyric Theatre, where an unprecedented extension of a beloved world is making something so impossible feel so much realer than it ever could be.
A theatrical tour de force...The production values are extraordinary.
And they might as well send out the 2018. Best Award for engraving already.
An unforgettable theatrical experience...The staging is simply magical.
The stagecraft is astonishing...Jamie Harrison's illusions are breathtaking...The play is long but never boring.

As winning as the Potter movies are, there’s something about seeing Rowling’s wizards, witches and Muggles—non-magical folk, in Potter parlance—presented in the flesh that drives home their essential, well, humanity.
Instead, Cursed Child spins the world of Harry Potter forward into a new generation, in a work of theatrical magic that has to be seen to be believed.
Tiffany is a wizard himself, navigating the emotional terrain with his own theatrical magic.
After a somewhat slow start, crammed with exposition, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 and 2 will have you in its spell.

The two-part, five-and-a-half-hour theatrical experience is an ambitious, effects-heavy spectacle that will dazzle Potter devotees — even if the story itself feels more like expensive fan fiction than a worthy sequel.
From there to the end, you will be fully immersed in what is truly a worthy follow-up to the extraordinary tale of Harry Potter, one that will speak to wizards, witches, and muggles alike.
The play still makes for a rousing adventure narrative.

The show is a marvel of stagecraft that manages to honor the source material while carving out its own distinct identity, even if the story itself feels more like expensive fan fiction than a worthy continuation of Rowling's saga.
It doesn’t take many speeches like that to bog down an already long show.

To commune with 1,000-plus fervent Harry Potter fans is to feel—in the best, most astonishing moments of this well-meaning, often silly, sometimes flat-out bad extravaganza—why theater is a wonderful medium for this ageless franchise.
As it stands, its effect more closely resembles a pack of Bertie Botts’s Every Flavor Beans — in which, too often, you draw the wrong flavor.
"Harry Potter and the Cursed Child" is an inspiration & celebration of one's imagination.
I hesitate to levy that judgement only because the inventiveness of this production seems better understood in another realm entirely.
"Harry Potter and the Cursed Child" is pure magic—an astonishing thrill ride packed with plentiful twists and turns in a production that marks a triumph of stagecraft.
A dazzling spectacle that brings magic to life on stage.
In a somewhat unmemorable Broadway season, the unprecedented magic of “Harry Potter and the Cursed Child” is the show to see and the one to try to beat come awards night.
A far cry from your typical Broadway brand extension, and in many ways...an improvement over the quality of the films.
It's a sensory overload that will have you hoping against hope that after all this time, your Hogwarts acceptance letter may still be just around the corner.

"The good news is that this somewhat overstuffed production is, in fact, a rip-roaring good yarn that actually seems like a continuation...Complex relationships, especially between parent and child and between friends are paramount to the two plays. Writing is sensitive and insightful. True to Rowling, rose-colored glasses are nowhere in sight...

The thing I like best about Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, which opened on Broadway on Sunday night, might be its title. The eponymous afflicted youth could be so many characters in the play. It could be Harry, now 40 and haunted by trauma and regret.
Be aware though, that all this does not mean that Cursed Child is a guaranteed audience pleaser for every theatergoer.
What Harry Potter and the Cursed Child lacks emotionally, it makes up for aesthetically, and it’s the creative team behind the show who are working real magic here.
On stage, the actors are utterly undistinguished.
It's by no means a great play but is certainly a great experience.
The problem for me was that I found the plot both convoluted and repetitious.

Except for the dazzling technical aspects of the production, I was put-off by the long, complicated and exceedingly dark story that has little apparent moral value – except to state the obvious – children need nurturing parents in order to become healthy adults.
For the rest of us the amusement is the magical stuff that makes descending chandeliers and flying Spidermen look like pikers.
This is a classic saga of parents and children and the things in life threatening to tear them apart.
An incredible theatrical experience...The magic is real on stage.

"Underneath all of the whimsy, cuteness, and nostalgia, this play is dark...Filled with action, humor, and adventure. The magic of the wizarding world is conveyed by a truly amazing combination of choreography, set design, and old-fashioned magic tricks...Not everything is perfect...
